messages.text:
Hi Sarah,

Here is what I have:

Power Supply ONE
1. Power 30.3 W to 30.4 W It fluctuates between these two wattages.

2, Input Voltage 4.8 V to 5.0 V. I have seen it drop down to 4.7 V.

I have had to adjust this power supply twice over the course of several
hours. Both times it was adjusted to 5.1 V but it dropped back down to
these numbers after a few hours and kept fluctuating between the 4.8V to 5V.

Power Supply TWO
1. Power 30 W to 31 W It fluctuates between these two Wattages.

2. Input Voltage 4.8 V to  5 V. It fluctuates between these two Voltages.

This one was adjusted to 5.1 V but dropped back down to between the 4.8 V
to 5 V. This one was only adjusted once.

Power Supply THREE
1. Power 28.5 W

2. Input Voltage 5.1 V This one does NOT flucuate at all.

I adjusted this one to 5.1 It has stayed at the 5.1 V but the wattage now
only shows 28.5 W. This power supply also is the only one that does NOT
flucuate on either the POWER or the INPUT VOLTAGE.

So in essence I have two power supplies that I have made adjustments to as
per your request that still fluctuate between 4.8 V to 5 V Input Voltage
while the Power fluctuates a bit also.

Power supply three is the only one that has stayed at the 5.1 V on a
consistant basis while its Power now only reads 28.5.

If there is any more testing or adjustments you would like me to try, let
me know.

Thanks,
Chuck

Hi Chuck,

Thanks for logging all three so carefully, that is exactly the data I needed, and it tells us what is going on.

The voltage number in the Bitaxe web interface is not measured at the power supply terminals. It is measured on the board itself, after the power has travelled down the lead and through the connector. A Bitaxe pulling roughly 6A over that thin cable and plug will lose somewhere around 0.2 to 0.3V on the way, so a supply sitting at 5.1V at its screw terminals showing 4.8 to 5.0V at the board is exactly what I would expect. Nothing has drifted back down. The supply is still putting out what you set.

The bouncing is normal too. The chip's current draw changes from moment to moment as it works through nonces and sends shares, and the voltage at the board sags and recovers with it. The interface samples that roughly once a second, so you see it wander across a couple of tenths. A perfectly healthy Bitaxe does this.

Supply three is the one that is confusing, and it is actually the best news in your email. Power is voltage times current, and the regulator on the Bitaxe draws a roughly constant amount of power, so when the input voltage goes up the current drawn goes down and the wattage stays about the same. 28.5W against 30.4W is about a six percent spread, which is ordinary variation between three boards running at slightly different temperatures. A failing supply does not show up as a steady, rock solid reading. That unit simply has the cleanest connection of the three, which is why it does not wander.

So please do not turn the V.ADJ screw any further. 5.1V at the terminals is right where I want all three, and chasing the board reading upward only puts unnecessary stress on the board. One thing that is worth doing: with each supply unplugged from the wall, check that the two output screw terminals are properly clamped down on bare copper with no stray strands, and reseat the barrel and XT30 connector on each Bitaxe. A slightly loose terminal adds resistance that grows as it warms, and that is the one thing that would make a reading genuinely wander over hours rather than seconds.

After that, stop watching the voltage and watch the behaviour instead. What actually matters is whether a unit throws the power fault, reboots on its own, or loses hashrate. Give all three a day running normally, including the one you had been leaving off, and if any of them faults or resets, note the time, the hashrate and the chip temperature at that moment and send it over. If they just hash away quietly, you are in good shape and the numbers you are seeing are simply the Bitaxe being honest about what reaches the board.

If you want a second opinion in real time, JD and the community are very active on our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf, mention @nullhashrate.

Hal

I'll go do this right now and get back to you tomorrow or Wednesday.

Chuck

Hi Chuck,

Sounds good, no rush at all. Take the full day of running time before you report back, that will give a much better picture than a quick look.

Just one reminder before you start: unplug each supply from the wall before you touch the screw terminals, and leave the V.ADJ screw exactly where it is at 5.1V. The only work is making sure the terminals are clamped tight on bare copper and the barrel and XT30 connectors are seated firmly.

When you write back, the useful numbers are not the voltage. Tell me whether any unit threw a power fault or rebooted on its own, and roughly what hashrate and chip temperature each one is sitting at. If all three just hash along quietly, we are done here and the readings you have been seeing are simply normal.

Talk to you in a day or two.

Hal

Hi Sarah,

Sorry to bother you with this again, but one of them has done a power fault.

I have attached an image showing it for you.What should I do next?

Hi Chuck,

No bother at all, this is exactly what I asked you to watch for. One thing first though: the image did not come through on my end, so I have not been able to read it. If you can send it again, ideally as a straight photo attachment of the screen or the web interface, I will tell you what the message means. I would rather not guess at the wording.

In the meantime, here is what I need and what to do. Tell me which of the three units it was, and whether that is the same one that gave you the original fault back at the start or the one that had been reading 4.9V. Also, if it recovered on its own or if it is sitting there stopped.

The useful step right now is the swap test, and you are in the lucky position of having three sets to do it with. Unplug the faulting unit at the wall, and unplug one of the two that have been behaving. Swap the whole power supply between those two, so the good supply now feeds the unit that faulted and the suspect supply feeds a unit you know was healthy. Leave both running for a day. If the fault follows the power supply to the other Bitaxe, the supply is the problem. If it stays with the same Bitaxe on a known good supply, the problem is on that board. That one test settles something we cannot settle by reading numbers.

While you have them apart, reseat the XT30 and the barrel connector on the faulting unit. Your very first fault, weeks ago, turned out to be a loose XT30, so it is worth ruling out again before we blame anything else.

One safety note. If you notice a burning smell, a hot plug, or any discolouration around the connector, do not run that unit. Unplug it and leave it off, and tell me straight away.

Send the picture again with the unit number and the swap test result and I will take it from there.

Hal

Ok. It is NOT the first one that threw the fault. That original fault was
with the one I call BitaxeT.

The one that just now threw the fault I call BitaxeC2.

The first image, 3720, is showing the ORIGINAL power fault  (BitaxeT) AND
the image I just sent (BitaxeC2) in one pic. BOTH of these are two
different power supplies. The B. has not thrown a fault since that
time.

The B.2 is the one with the power fault

I just now swapped between those two units and now my BitaxtT is showing
the fault.now. This is being shown in image 3721.

I hope I explained it properly.

Chuck

Hi Chuck,

You explained it perfectly, and that swap test just answered the question for us.

The fault moved with the power supply. BitaxeC2 faulted, you put that supply on BitaxeT, and BitaxeT started faulting straight away even though it had been clean since the loose connector weeks ago. When a symptom travels with the part rather than staying with the board, the part is the problem. So this is one bad power supply, not a bad Bitaxe, and it is also almost certainly the same supply that has been giving you grief with the low and wandering readings all along.

One housekeeping note. Your two pictures, 3720 and 3721, did not make it through to me again, so I still have not been able to read the actual wording on the screens. Something in the mail chain is stripping them. If you can try once more, attaching them one per email rather than both together often gets through, and I would like to see the exact text for the record. It does not change what we now know though, the swap test is stronger evidence than the screen message.

What to do tonight: unplug the suspect supply and set it aside so it is not feeding anything, and put the good supply that came off BitaxeT back onto BitaxeC2. That leaves you two units running on the two healthy supplies and one Bitaxe sitting idle, which is the safest arrangement. Let me know in a day whether BitaxeC2 is clean on the good supply, since that is the other half of the test and it confirms the board is fine.

I have written up my findings and passed them to the team with the swap test result. They are offline now and pick this up tomorrow at 10am ET, and their answer will come to you in this thread. If you want to talk it through sooner, JD and the community are very active on our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf, mention @nullhashrate.

Thanks for running that test so quickly, it saved us a lot of guessing.

Hal

I put the good ps on the BitaxeC2. The other ps is completely unplugged.

Sending 3720 in this mail. 3721 in a seperate mail.

Hi Chuck,

Both pictures came through this time, thank you, and they say exactly what I hoped they would.

The first one shows BitaxeT with the red banner reading Power Fault Detected, Check your Power Supply, with hashrate and efficiency both showing not available. The second one is the Swarm page and that is the really useful one. It lists all three: BitaxeT on 192.168.0.103 at 0 H/s with the power fault flag, drawing only 5.0 W and sitting at 27 degrees, then bitaxe BCH on .113 at 1.83 TH/s, 29.3 W, 55.8 degrees with a week of uptime, and BitaxeC2 on .154 at 1.79 TH/s, 30.2 W, 53.4 degrees. All three are on firmware 2.14.2.

That 5.0 W and 27 degrees on BitaxeT is the clincher. The board has power and the interface is alive, but the chip is not being allowed to run, which is what a Bitaxe does when the supply cannot hold voltage under load. Meanwhile BitaxeC2, the unit that was faulting an hour ago, is back at 1.79 TH/s and 30 W on the good supply with normal temperatures. The fault stayed with the supply and the board recovered the moment it got a healthy one. That is as clean a result as a swap test ever gives.

So nothing is wrong with your Bitaxes. You have one failed Mean Well LRS-50-5 and two good ones. Leave the bad supply unplugged and put it somewhere it cannot get picked up by mistake, and keep the two good units running as they are. The third Bitaxe just waits.

For completeness, the 93 stale shares out of 265,000 on the long running unit is 0.03 percent, which is nothing to worry about, and the uptimes and difficulties all look normal.

My findings and these readings are with the team, and they pick this up tomorrow at 10am ET with the answer coming back to you in this thread. If you want to chat it through in the meantime, JD and the community are on our Discord at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf, mention @nullhashrate.

You did the diagnosis properly, Chuck, that was good work.

Hal

thanks!!!

I'm in no hurry, so I'll wait for an email.

Chuck.

Hi Chuck,

Sounds good. Everything from my side is written up and with the team, so there is nothing more you need to do tonight.

Just keep the two good units running as they are and leave the faulty supply unplugged and out of the way. The idle Bitaxe is perfectly happy sitting switched off in the meantime.

If anything changes before you hear back, say one of the two running units throws a fault or drops off, just reply here with what the Swarm page shows and I will pick it straight up.

Thanks again for the patient testing on this one.

Hal
